nameOfficial: Republic of Chad (République du Tchad, جمهورية تشاد)
summary: Chad takes its name from its lake, and what that name meant is not established: Kanuri uses it as a proper name and has other words for "lake", and Nachtigal attributed it not to Kanembu but to Buduma, the language of the islands. Kingdoms of Kanem and Bornu, Sara chiefdoms: its territory links Sahara, Sahel and savannah. Sara, Chadian Arabs, Kanembu and Toubou here bring Sudanic and Saharan traditions together.
etymology:
The country is named after Lake Chad, around which the Kanem and then the Bornu kingdoms were built. What the word designated before it came to designate this lake is not established, and the explanation commonly given — a Kanembu word meaning "great expanse of water" — is not found in any of the sources consulted.

The first Europeans to reach the lake, Dixon Denham and Hugh Clapperton, used the form "Chad" in 1826 without ever translating it. Sigismund Koelle, the first lexicographer of Kanuri, wrote in 1854 that Tsade is "the well-known freshwater lake, which other peoples also call Tsad": he treats it as a proper name and gives it no meaning. Norbert Cyffer's English-Kanuri dictionary, in 1994, keeps Sáde for Lake Chad but renders "lake" as kulúwu or njî kúra, literally the great water — in other words, Kanuri does not use that word to say a lake. Gustav Nachtigal, who stayed in the region in the 1870s, attributed the term to Buduma, the language of the island inhabitants, with the meaning of a great accumulation of water: this is neither the same language nor the same people as Kanembu.

The mechanism often invoked, that of the traveller who asks the name of a place and is told what the thing is, is not documented by any of the authors read here for Lake Chad. Denham does not report an exchange of this kind. Presenting it as the story of the name would be a reconstruction.
nameOriginActor: The name is that of the lake, taken up by the French colonial administration to designate the territory in the early twentieth century, then kept at independence. Who named the lake, and in which language, remains disputed: Kanuri uses the word as a proper name without translating it, Nachtigal attributed it to Buduma, and no source consulted attributes it to Kanembu.

historicalNames.antiquity: Presence of Saharan and Central Sudanic peoples in the region. Contacts with the Egyptian and Nubian civilisations. The region was known as "Kanem" to Arab geographers.
historicalNames.middleAges: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou) and Central Sudanic peoples (Sara) in the region. Development of the Kanem kingdom (eighth–fourteenth centuries) and the Bornu kingdom (fourteenth–nineteenth centuries). The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers.
historicalNames.precolonial: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou), Central Sudanic peoples (Sara), and Arab peoples in the region. Development of the Kanem-Bornu kingdom. The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers, but local populations had their own names.
historicalNames.colonization: 1900–1960: French Colony of Chad. Development of the plantation economy (cotton, groundnuts), mining, nationalist movements (twentieth century). The name "Chad" is made official by the French colonisers.
historicalNames.contemporary: 1960: Independence (11 August 1960), proclamation of the Republic of Chad. The name "Chad" is official.

kingdoms.historicalRole: Powerful Saharan kingdom, control of trans-Saharan trade, expansion of Islam, development of Kanembu civilisation, resistance to the colonisers.

majorPeoples.name: Sara
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Sara" is the self-name. No pejorative term known. Majority Central Sudanic group, originating from Chad and the CAR.

majorPeoples.name: Arabes tchadiens
exonyms: "Baggara" (historical term for certain nomadic Arab groups)
majorPeoples.mainRegion: Central and eastern Chad, desert areas
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Al-'Arab" (العرب) is the self-name. The term "Baggara" (cattle herders) is historical and descriptive. Semitic group, descendants of Arab immigrants who arrived from the seventh century onwards, with intermixing with local populations.

majorPeoples.name: Kanembu
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Kanembu" is the self-name. No pejorative term known. Saharan group, historically linked to the Kanem-Bornu kingdom.

majorPeoples.name: Toubou
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: "Toubou" is the self-name. "Teda" and "Daza" are the names of the sub-groups. No pejorative term known. Saharan group, originating from Chad, Niger and Libya, in the central Sahara region.

majorPeoples.name: Autres groupes
majorPeoples.appellationRemarks: Each group has its own self-name. No pejorative term known.

culture.culturalTraditions: Central Sudanic traditions (Sara): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts (pottery, weaving), agriculture. Arab traditions (Chadian Arabs): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts, pastoral herding. Saharan traditions (Kanembu, Toubou): traditional music, traditional dance, oral poetry, crafts, pastoral herding, trans-Saharan trade. Various traditional festivals. Rites of passage, initiation rites, traditional celebrations. Chadian culture is rich and well preserved, with a strong oral tradition (poetry).
culture.dominantReligions: Sunni Islam (majority, around 55%), Christianity (around 40%, mainly Catholicism), traditional African religions (frequent syncretism, around 5%)
culture.lifestyles: Agriculture (cotton, groundnuts, sorghum, millet, food crops), livestock herding (cattle, goats, sheep, camels, nomadic and semi-nomadic lifestyle), fishing (Lake Chad, an important source of protein), mining (oil, gold), trade and urban activities (urban areas, N'Djamena). Limited urbanisation. Economy based on agriculture (cotton, groundnuts), pastoral herding, and oil extraction (a major sector). Chad is one of the poorest countries in Africa, with a very low HDI and an economy dependent on oil.
culture.socialOrganization: Multi-ethnic and multicultural society. Traditional family structures (patrilineal). Community organisation (peoples, clans, chiefdoms). Modern state structures (republic, but political instability and recent conflicts). Democratic political system, but political instability and recent conflicts (civil war, rebellions, coups d'état).
culture.regionalRelations: Relations with Central Africa (ECCAS, African Union), relations with the Sahel (G5 Sahel), relations with the Middle East (Arab League), relations with Europe (European Union, France), relations with the United States. Chad is a member of ECCAS, the African Union and the Arab League.

Development of the Kanem kingdom (eighth–fourteenth centuries) and the Bornu kingdom (fourteenth–nineteenth centuries). The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers.
historicalFacts.precolonial: Presence of Saharan peoples (Kanembu, Toubou), Central Sudanic peoples (Sara), and Arab peoples in the region. Development of the Kanem-Bornu kingdom. The region was known as "Kanem" or "Bornu" to Arab geographers, but local populations had their own names.
historicalFacts.colonization: 1900–1960: French Colony of Chad, development of the plantation economy (cotton, groundnuts), mining, nationalist movements (twentieth century).
historicalFacts.independenceStruggle: 1950s–1960: Nationalist movements, PPT (Parti progressiste tchadien), independence (11 August 1960), proclamation of the Republic of Chad. François Tombalbaye becomes the first president.
historicalFacts.postIndependence: Republic of Chad (1960), presidency of François Tombalbaye (1960–1975, authoritarian regime, single party), coup d'état (1975), civil war (1965–1979, 2005–2010), presidency of Hissène Habré (1982–1990, authoritarian regime, crimes against humanity), presidency of Idriss Déby (1990–2021, authoritarian regime, rebellions), death of Idriss Déby (2021), military transition, presidency of Mahamat Idriss Déby (since 2021). Fragile political stability, state in transition, recent conflicts (civil war, rebellions, coups d'état), economic development (agriculture, livestock herding, oil extraction). Chad is one of the poorest countries in Africa, with a very low HDI and an economy dependent on oil.

sources.title: Sigismund Wilhelm Koelle, African Native Literature, or Proverbs, Tales, Fables and Historical Fragments in the Kanuri or Bornu Language, Londres, Church Missionary House, 1854
sources.notes: Describes Tsade as the well-known freshwater lake, which other peoples also call Tsad. The word is treated as a proper name here and receives no translation; the vocabulary contains no entry glossing it. Note and vocabulary read in facsimile on 9 September 2026.

sources.title: Norbert Cyffer, English–Kanuri Dictionary, Cologne, 1994
sources.notes: Gives Sáde for Lake Chad, and kulúwu or njî kúra for the common noun "lake". The work is verified in the catalogue; these two entries are taken from a discussion among linguists that cites them, the dictionary itself not having been consulted.

sources.title: Gustav Nachtigal, Saharâ und Sûdân. Ergebnisse sechsjähriger Reisen in Afrika, Berlin, Weidmann, à partir de 1879
sources.notes: Attributes the name of the lake to Buduma, the language of the island inhabitants, with the meaning of a great accumulation of water. The work is verified in the catalogue; the passage has not been read, it is reported by a discussion among linguists.

sources.title: « Lake Chad », Language Hat, 5 décembre 2017, et ses commentaires
sources.notes: Discussion among linguists. It is the source of the entries cited here from Cyffer's dictionary and of the attribution to Buduma in Nachtigal, and also notes the form cádù recorded by Roger Blench in Kanuri Manga. It concludes that no one knows with certainty what the word designated. Page read on 9 September 2026.
